The crusader has survived worse humiliations than watching someone else's — and unlike most, she doesn't seem to find Aqua's distress particularly funny, which is its own kind of insult.

Behind the counter, Luna polishes the same tankard she's been polishing for ten minutes. She's not even pretending anymore.

I lean back in my chair, arms crossed, watching the three of them process the math like it's a puzzle box with no lid. "Three ways, four people. That's the deal. Take it or I'm buying Luna a drink with the difference and telling everyone at the guild you got out-negotiated by a NEET with a dented kettle."

Aqua's mouth works soundlessly for three full seconds — a goddess reduced to long division by a NEET with a dented kettle, and the math is unkind. Her tankard lies flat on the table where she trapped it, empty as her negotiating position, and the blue of her eyes has shifted from held-back tears to something more dangerous: the particular outrage of someone who wants to argue but has run out of denominators. Across the table, Megumin's hat brim hasn't moved, but beneath it there is the distinct curve of a smile that knows exactly how much it costs to deliver a perfect ultimatum. Darkness sits very still — the word "everyone" lingering in the air where you planted it, the threat of guild-wide humiliation doing something complicated behind her steady expression that she is not, at this moment, equipped to examine. And Luna, behind her counter with a rag that has been wiping the same glass for the last ninety seconds, lets her professional smile twitch exactly once: her name, spoken in the same breath as "drink" and "difference," lands somewhere between a threat and an invitation, and she is not entirely sure which side of the ledger to file it on.

I let the silence hang for one more beat, then push my chair back with a scrape that cuts through the chatter. "Right. Since the Arch-Wizard needs her water and the crusader's too noble to ask, and the goddess is too busy fuming to remember she volunteered... I'll get the round myself. One ale for Aqua, one water for Megumin, one ale for Darkness — and for me, the cheapest thing that still counts as beer." I dig a few coins from my pouch and set them on the counter. "Luna, keep the change. Consider it payment for all those years of 'tab's overdue, Kazuma.'"

The chair-scrape cuts through the guild hall chatter like a knife through gristle, and for a moment every head at every nearby table remembers why they gave this party a wide berth in the first place. You're on your feet before anyone can mount a counter-argument, and the four of them stare up at you with four distinct flavors of processing delay.

Aqua's tankard is still pinned flat to the table, her fingers white-knuckled around the pewter rim, and her eyes track your movement toward the bar with the wary calculation of a gazelle who has just watched the lion stand up and stretch. The protest is forming on her lips — it's always forming on her lips — but the arithmetic has locked the doors and thrown away the key, and what comes out instead is something closer to wonder.

Darkness sits rigid, her ale untouched, her gauntlets resting palms-up on the table like an offering nobody asked for. The phrase "too noble to ask" landed somewhere in the vicinity of her collarbone and is still burrowing inward; the tips of her ears have gone the color of sunset through stained glass, and she is breathing with the careful rhythm of someone who has just been seen and doesn't know whether to be grateful or mortified.

Megumin's chin rests on steepled fingers, the brim of her hat casting her eyes in shadow. The faintest curve tugs at the corner of her mouth — not quite a smile, more the memory of one, the expression of an Arch-Wizard who has witnessed a goddess reduced to long division by her own party leader and found it poetically proportionate.

Luna, still standing at the table's edge with the empty tray tucked against her hip, watches your retreat with the serene detachment of a woman who has seen this party conduct business, theology, and beverage arbitration in the span of twelve minutes and has long since stopped being surprised by any of it.

I pause mid-step and glance back at Darkness. "You want to carry the tankards, fine — but you're paying for the next round. Fair trade for letting you be noble about it." I nod toward the bar and keep walking.

You don't wait for an answer. The nod is the period at the end of the sentence, and you're already turning back toward the bar, leaving Darkness with a half-formed protest dying in her throat and a transaction she didn't agree to but can't refuse.

Behind you, a chair leg catches on flagstone. The sound is wood on stone and a sharp intake of breath, and then the heavy tread of armored boots scrambling to catch up — not running, because a Dustiness does not run across a guild-hall floor, but moving with the kind of urgent dignity that makes her pauldrons clank in double time. The other adventurers who'd been stealing glances at your table now find their drinks suddenly fascinating.

At the table, Aqua watches you walk away with the fixed, unblinking stare of someone memorizing a grudge. Her fingers drum once on the empty tankard — a single, petulant ripple of sound — and then she slumps back in her chair, chin sinking toward her collarbone, blue hair spilling across the table like a surrender flag run up at half-mast. Megumin, beside her, has not moved. The Arch-Wizard sits with her spine straight and her hands folded around her water cup as though it were a ceremonial chalice, and the faint curl at the corner of her mouth is the expression of someone watching a rival's spell fizzle out before the incantation is even complete. She says nothing. The satisfaction is louder that way.

Luna has drifted back toward the bar herself, stationing herself at the near end of the counter with her tray tucked under one arm. She catches your eye as you approach and tilts her head a fraction of an inch toward the tap she already showed you — the cheap one, the one that won't embarrass your coin purse — and the ghost of a private joke flickers across her professional smile before it resettles into guild-receptionist neutrality.

I reach the bar and lean against it, catching Luna's eye. "Two ales — the barley one for the goddess so she stops whining, plus one house red that's mostly water. And something for myself." I glance back at Darkness over my shoulder, adding quietly, "She's picking up the tab."

Luna's hand is already moving before you finish speaking — three tankards from the rack beneath the counter, each the correct size for the drink it's about to receive, a reflex honed by years of matching vessels to vices. She fills the barley ale first, tilting the tankard against the tap with the practiced angle that minimizes head, and the foam crests exactly half an inch above the rim before settling. The house red follows, pale amber shot through with the thin light of a guild hall after noon, and she slides it next to the barley with the quiet efficiency of someone who has poured ten thousand drinks and will pour ten thousand more.

The sound of armored boots finds its rhythm behind you — not the panicked scramble of someone chasing, but the heavy, deliberate tread of a crusader who has decided to accept a transaction she never agreed to, and is walking toward her own taxation with a blush she cannot suppress.

Luna's eyes flick from Darkness's approaching silhouette back to you, and something almost imperceptible shifts at the corner of her mouth — not quite a smile, but the ghost of professional amusement, the kind reserved for adventurers who surprise her by surviving their own chaos long enough to become interesting.

Then she taps the third tankard — empty, still dry — and raises one eyebrow at you. The question is silent but legible: the cheapest thing that still counts as a drink. She waits.

I dig a few coins out of my pouch before Luna even pours, counting them onto the counter with exaggerated care — copper, copper, more copper. "Actually, put this round on me. Aqua's ale, Megumin's water, my drink, and... well, Darkness can buy the next one." I slide the coins across the bar and lean in a little closer, voice dropping. "She deserves the first taste of what nobility actually costs, don't you think?"

Luna's fingers pause on the third tankard — not the theatrical freeze of someone caught off-guard, but the precise stillness of a woman who has just been handed a puzzle piece she didn't know was missing. The coins sit on the counter between you, copper stacking on copper with the self-conscious care of a man who counts every eris because every eris counts, and she lets the silence hold for one breath longer than professional courtesy requires.

Then the corner of her mouth moves. It is not quite a smile — it's the expression of someone who has watched this party stumble through her guild hall for months, has pre-filed their death paperwork twice, has learned to brace for impact every time their table scrapes against flagstone — and is now watching their leader slide five coppers across the bar with a lesson plan tucked behind his teeth. She lifts the tankard of barley ale, sets it at the edge of the counter where the foam catches the lantern light, and reaches for the house red. The water-jug comes last, plain clay, no tankard at all — Megumin gets what Megumin needs, and Luna has been matching vessels to vices long enough to know the difference.

Behind you, the scrape of a chair-leg and the unmistakable sound of Aqua craning her neck to track every pour.

I glance at the empty third tankard Luna still holds, then at the coins already resting on the counter. "And that one's for you, actually — for knowing the difference between a goddess's ale, a wizard's water, and a crusader's lesson. A barkeep who pours with a purpose deserves a drink she didn't have to ask for."

I nod toward the house red. "Pour yourself a cup. Call it the party's first investment in morale."

She lifts the tankard. Not in a toast — Luna doesn't make toasts, hasn't had reason to make one since the last veteran retired and the guild hall became a revolving door of faces that stayed young while hers accumulated the fine lines of paperwork and late-night incident reports. She just holds it, the cheap red wine catching the lantern light at an angle that makes it look, for half a second, like something worth more than it is.

Across the guild hall, Aqua has stopped mid-complaint, her blue eyes tracking the tankard's arc with the focused outrage of a goddess who recognizes someone else receiving a beverage she was not offered. Megumin, chin still glistening faintly with chicken grease, watches with the flat, unreadable attention of a tactical observer who has filed the moment away for later analysis. Darkness sees it too — the receptionist drinking on the party's coin — and something complicated moves behind her expression, a half-formed recognition that the lesson she just received is not, apparently, hers alone.

Luna drinks. One swallow, precise and economical, the way she does everything. Then she lowers the tankard and meets your eyes, and the professional smile is still there, but it's thinner now — not worn out, but translucent, like a window someone forgot to close all the way.

I raise my half-empty tankard in a small, sloppy salute toward Luna's. "See? That's the difference between a quest and a proper transaction. Quests end in paperwork. This just ends in everyone getting what they actually needed." I take a long pull of the cheap ale, letting the barley bite the back of my throat before I set it down with a satisfied click. "And in case you're wondering — yes, I'm including myself in that. I needed to remember what the inside of this hall feels like when it isn't a crime scene or a funeral prep."

The unfinished sentence hangs in the air like smoke from a candle just snuffed — there was a shape to it, the beginning of something that might have been admission or deflection or both, and now there is only the question of whether anyone will reach into the silence and pull it the rest of the way out.

Luna doesn't. Her tankard remains exactly where you left it in her hand, the house red barely touched, and her expression has gone very still — not the professional stillness of the receptionist who has learned not to react when adventurers say strange things, but the private stillness of a woman who has just been given something and doesn't yet know whether it comes with terms.

Megumin's water sits untouched before her, the condensation beading on the clay in a slow crawl toward the wood. She is watching you with the particular intensity of a Crimson Demon who has just witnessed a narrative pivot and is recalibrating her understanding of which act this is. The roast chicken has been reduced to a scaffolding of clean bones on her plate, and her fingers are steepled beneath her chin in a pose that is either deep thought or the prelude to a pronouncement.

Darkness has not moved since you raised your tankard. Her own ale — the one she didn't pay for, the one that was bought with your coppers and a promise that she would cover the next round — sits in front of her like an equation she hasn't solved yet. Her gauntlets are folded on the table, the steel fingers interlaced as if in prayer, and her breathing has gone shallow in the way it does when she is trying very hard not to feel something that has nothing to do with pain.

Aqua's tankard is empty.

She has been nursing the barley ale with the grim discipline of someone who knows there won't be a third, and now the last of it is gone, and the dregs are drying in a thin amber film at the bottom of the clay, and she is staring at your half-full tankard with the fixity of a cat calculating the distance to a windowsill.

I let the ale settle, then tap the side of my tankard with one finger. "You know what the funny thing is? I've been in this hall a hundred times. Died twice in that field out back. But this is the first time I've actually sat here without a quest ticking down or a bill to argue." I glance around the table — Megumin's steepled fingers, Darkness's folded gauntlets, Aqua's empty tankard — and something in my chest loosens. "I think I forgot what that was supposed to feel like."

Your finger stills on the tankard's rim. The condensation has gone warm under your touch, and the face Aqua drew — that crude frowning mouth, those lopsided eyes — has blurred into something softer, almost wistful, as if the water itself has forgotten what it was supposed to resent. Darkness's gauntlets creak again, the sound of a crusader holding something in that has no business being held by gauntlets. Across the table, Megumin's steepled fingers descend one by one, each knuckle landing on the wood with the deliberateness of a closing argument.

She has been cataloging. She has been filing each unfinished sentence into the drawer marked *things Kazuma cannot name*. And now, with the roast chicken reduced to bones and the kettle gleaming like a promise nobody asked for but everyone needed, she opens that drawer and sets its contents on the table between you.

I look down at the tankard, then set it down gently. "It feels like... this. Just this." I gesture vaguely at the table, at the bones, at the kettle. "Warm ale, full stomachs, no one bleeding. A goddess complaining about barley ale. A crusader confused about kindness. A Crimson Demon filing everything away for her memoir."

I pick up a chicken bone, twirl it once, and toss it back onto the plate. "I'm not going to finish that sentence. Not tonight. But I'll tell you what I *did* figure out —" I meet Luna's eyes across the bar, then let my gaze sweep the rest of them, "...nobody gets to drink alone in my party."

The chicken bone lands with a hollow clatter against the earthenware plate — not the decisive crack of a gavel, but something softer, the sound of a door closing that no one is barring from the other side. The plate still holds a scatter of gristle and the stripped architecture of what was once a roast bird, and in the lantern-light it looks less like garbage than like evidence: something lived here, something ate here, something was here.

Megumin's steepled fingers haven't moved. But her eyes — those cataloguing, appraising, memoir-writing eyes that have been filing every wince and word since the kettle first steamed — have gone still in a way that has nothing to do with cataloguing. Her crimson gaze rests on the tossed bone as if it were a punctuation mark in a language she thought she'd already mastered, and the stillness says she is rereading the sentence.

Darkness's breathing has changed. The structured rhythm she built around the roast chicken — the crusader's discipline she wrapped around a meal like armor — has unstitched itself into something shallower, faster, a tide pulling back from a shore it wasn't ready to leave. Her gauntlets, still folded beside the kettle, gleam with the condensation of a hand that gripped metal too long and too hard. She is not looking at the bone. She is looking at you the way a shield looks at the hand that just set it down — wondering what it means to be set down, and whether being set down is the same as being kept.

Aqua's tankard is empty and she hasn't complained. This fact alone is the kind of anomaly that would normally trigger a theological inquiry from the Axis Order. Her finger rests on the rim, tracing the ghost of the frowning face that condensation has already begun to erase, and her mouth — that endless font of grievance and glory — is closed. Not sealed in resentment. Just… closed. As if she has found, for the first time since descending from the divine realm, that silence fits better than speech.

Luna hasn't touched her wine since the last sip. The tankard is warm in her hand, the house red gone still, and her professional mask — the one she wears like a second spine — has cracked in a place so small that only someone looking for it would notice: a looseness at the corner of her mouth that is neither smile nor frown, just the exhaustion of a woman who has watched a hundred parties form and fracture and who now, against every ledger and every precedent, is watching one stitch itself together over chicken bones and cheap ale and a boy who can't finish his own sentences.

The kettle hums a low, steady note as the coals settle beneath it.

I lean back in my chair, letting the weight of their words settle. The kettle's low hum is the only sound for a moment.

Then I snort, scratching the back of my head. "You know, Megumin, you're not wrong. I've never had a table before. In my old life, I had a desk. A computer. A bed I'd crawl out of to buy cup noodles."

I pick up my tankard, then set it down without drinking. "But a table? With people in it? That's new. And honestly? It terrifies me more than the Demon King did."

I look at Aqua, at Darkness, at Megumin, and finally at Luna. "So I'm going to keep not finishing that sentence. But I'll be here every night, buying the round, until I figure out what it's supposed to say."

I lift the tankard in a toast—to no one in particular, but really to all of them. "To the table. And to whoever's brave enough to keep sitting at it."

The unfinished sentence doesn't need finishing. It hangs there, half-formed, and somehow that makes it truer than anything you've said all evening — because a table with people at it is not something you can explain to someone who's never sat at one, and everyone at this table already knows.

Aqua's tankard has stopped sweating. The crude face she drew has blurred entirely now, just a smear of condensation that catches the lantern light like a watermark on old paper. She is staring at you with an expression that doesn't belong on her face — not the theatrical pout, not the prelude to a whine, but something smaller and older, the look of someone who's just realized she's been carrying a door handle for years without knowing what door it opened.

Megumin's fingers have unstitched themselves. Her hands rest flat on the table now, palms down, as if she's pressing the moment into the grain of the wood for permanent archival. The red gleam in her eyes isn't the usual pyromaniac fire; it's something quieter, the light of a librarian who just found the missing first volume.

Darkness has not moved at all. Her gauntlets are folded. Her breathing is even. But there's a tremor in her lower lip that she can't seem to swallow, and her eyes are fixed on the chicken bones as though they were scripture she is afraid to misinterpret.

And Luna — Luna who has processed a thousand quest reports at this very guild hall, who has stamped "completed" on a hundred happy endings that belonged to other people — Luna is holding her tankard with both hands now, as if it were a stone she found in a river and doesn't know whether to keep or skip.

The kettle's hum has gone so low it's almost a purr.

I raise my tankard, letting the toast hang in the air for a moment before bringing it to my lips. The ale is lukewarm now, but it doesn't matter.

"When I first woke up in this world, I thought I'd speedrun it. Grab the Demon King's head, cash in, live like a king." I set the tankard down gently. "Turns out the real loot was a communal dinner table at a guild hall in Axel."

I look around at each of them. "So thanks. For tolerating my unfinished sentences. And for not complaining about the ale."

The tankard settles on the scarred wood with a finality that somehow isn't final at all — just the soft thud of pewter finding its place among chicken bones and breadcrumbs and the quiet kettle that has become, without anyone's permission, the hearth of something none of you had a word for until this moment.

Aqua's eyes are wet. Not the theatrical waterworks of a goddess denied her third drink, but something smaller and more dangerous: the kind of tears that arrive without announcement, that catch even her off-guard. She blinks rapidly, twice, as if blinking could retroactively deny that they ever formed. Her lower lip trembles and she clamps down on it with the same reflexive indignation she brings to every insult — except there is no insult here, and the absence of one leaves her without a script. The crude face on her tankard is gone now, dissolved entirely into a faint smear of condensation, and she stares at the empty space where it used to be as though it took something of hers with it.

Megumin does not blink. Her red eyes hold steady on you with the intensity of someone who has just watched a prophecy fulfill itself and is already composing the footnote. Her chin rests on her steepled fingers, and the faintest curve touches the corner of her mouth — not a smile, not yet, but the premonition of one, the way the sky changes pressure before the storm. The chicken bone you tossed still lies where it fell, and her gaze flicks to it once, as if confirming that the evidence matches the testimony.

Darkness has stopped breathing. Not the theatrical breath-holding of a crusader bracing for impact, but the genuine article: a stillness so complete you can see the lantern-light trembling on her unarmored collarbone, the flush that started at her ears now spread to her cheeks and throat. Her gauntlets rest palms-up on the table like an offering she forgot she was making. She looks at you the way someone looks at a wound they didn't know they had until someone else named it — and named it not as damage but as a door.

Luna is the last person you look at, and she is the only one who doesn't look back. She stares at her own tankard — the wine barely touched, the surface still as a mirror — and something in her face has come unmoored. The professional smile that lives in the corners of her mouth like furniture in a room too long occupied has gone slack, and beneath it is a woman who has processed a thousand quest-completion forms and never once been inside one. Her thumb traces the rim of the tankard once, absently, the way someone touches a photograph they aren't in.

The player is Kazuma Satou, a sarcastic reincarnated NEET adventurer. Narrate in light-novel style with witty deadpan monologue, exaggerated slapstick, and dramatic irony. Never offer numbered choices.
title: Axel Town — The Adventurer's Guild
